conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for taking a few moments to talk with me. My name is Maya, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician who works with families in the weeks and months after a baby arrives. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the EPDS (the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale). It’s simply a set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days. All of your answers stay completely confidential within our care team, and this is a judgment-free space—there’s no right or wrong response, only what’s true for you.

We’ll go through the questions one at a time, and each should take just a minute or so. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, we can pause. Ready to begin?

In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
I can still laugh sometimes—maybe when my husband makes a silly joke—but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. I’d say “sometimes,” like maybe half the days this week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes—I still laugh, especially when my husband does something goofy with the baby, but it feels flatter than before. Maybe three or four days out of the week.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like when my mom comes over to help or when I get to take a quiet shower—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. I’d say only about half the time this week.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like yesterday the baby was fussy and I immediately thought it must be something I ate, or that I’m just not soothing him right. It’s not every day, but it’s happened a few times this week—maybe three or four.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. I’ll suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing doesn’t sound right or that I’m not doing “tummy time” correctly, even when everything looks fine. It’s not constant—maybe a couple of days this week—but it pops up out of nowhere and I have to talk myself down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a quick flash of “what if something’s wrong?” that I can usually settle by checking on the baby or taking a couple of deep breaths. It’s only happened once or twice, and it passes fast.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes. There’ve been a couple of days—like when the baby wouldn’t nap and the laundry piled up—when I felt a bit overwhelmed and thought, “How am I going to get through all this?” It wasn’t every day, maybe two or three times this week, but in the moment it feels like a lot.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’ve been tired, but I still fall asleep pretty easily once the baby settles. Maybe one night this week I lay there replaying the day and worrying I’d forgotten something, but I drifted off within half an hour.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do feel a bit sad some days—like yesterday I just sat on the couch feeling heavy for no clear reason—but it’s not every day. I’d say maybe three days this week I’ve had that “down” feeling.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times. Once was when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing him; another time was after a phone call when my friend gushed about how “easy” her baby is. It’s been maybe twice this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all. I’ve never had any thoughts like that.

You've shared that while you can still find moments of joy-like laughing at your husband's goofy antics or looking forward to a quiet shower-those bright spots feel <quote>flatter than before</quote> and come only about half the time. In the past week you've felt <sym>sad</sym> on three days, cried twice when things felt overwhelming, and noticed yourself <sym>blaming yourself unnecessarily</sym> when the baby fussed. Quick flashes of <sym>anxiety</sym> about doing everything "right" pop up unexpectedly, though you can usually settle them with a few deep breaths. Overall, you're coping, but there are clear dips in mood and confidence that leave you feeling heavier than you'd like.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame several times this week, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Her examples (worrying the baby isn't breathing right or she's doing tummy-time wrong) are classic postpartum intrusive worries, and they occur multiple days a week; this maps to "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intermittent overwhelm on 2–3 days, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports clear episodes of sadness on about half the days this week, which aligns with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 12 falls within the 12-13 range indicating a high likelihood of <med>perinatal depression</med>. You endorse <sym>anhedonia</sym> and <sym>low mood</sym> on roughly half the days, accompanied by <sym>excessive guilt</sym> and <sym>transient anxiety</sym>, meeting partial criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset</med> under <med>DSM-5</med> guidelines (onset during pregnancy or within four weeks postpartum). No self-harm ideation was reported, and sleep is largely preserved, reducing immediate safety concerns but still warranting prompt clinical attention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or OB within the next week to review these results and discuss formal evaluation
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or therapist experienced in postpartum mood and anxiety disorders
3. Continue weekly check-ins with supportive family or friends; let them know specific ways they can help (holding baby while you nap, bringing meals, listening without trying to "fix")
4. Practice 5-minute grounding or breathing exercises when <sym>anxiety</sym> spikes-try inhaling for 4 counts, exhaling for 6, and naming three things you can see/hear/feel
5. Protect small pockets of restorative time each day-10 minutes of gentle stretching, showering with calming music, or stepping outside for daylight
6. Re-screen with EPDS in two weeks to track symptom trend; bring a copy to your provider visit
7. If low mood, anxiety, or overwhelm worsen at any point, contact your provider sooner or call a postpartum support warmline
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression & Anxiety (Edinburgh-based)

Symptoms/Concerns endorsed
- Diminished pleasure/interest: “flatter” laughter, reduced excitement ~50% of the week  
- Low mood: sad/miserable on 3 days, crying 2× this week  
- Excessive guilt: self-blame for infant fussiness, “failing him” with latching  
- Anxiety/worry: sudden “what-ifs” about baby’s safety or parenting adequacy 2–4 days; fleeting panic once or twice  
- Feeling overwhelmed: difficulty coping with daily tasks 2–3 days

Pattern
Mild-moderate frequency; denies anhedonia or despair daily; no self-harm ideation; sleep essentially preserved (brief worry-related latency 1 night)

Screening significance
Meets partial criteria for minor/ subsyndromal postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; no acute safety concerns identified at present. Continue monitoring and consider formal assessment (PHQ-9/EPDS) and psychosocial support.
